title: Building a Tree That Is Its Own Blueprint
concept_layer: recursion as a form-generating function applied to its own output; self-similarity; depth as the bounded parameter of an otherwise infinite structure

capture_leaks.finite_depth: Real fractals are infinite by definition. Depth 3 is practical; depth 20 crashes the engine. The map fakes infinity by implying it.
capture_leaks.discrete_branching: A real tree doesn’t choose between 2 branches — it produces however many buds a meristem activates. Procgen tree artifacts handle continuous branching.
capture_leaks.no_physics: Branches can't sag, bend, snap, or grow. They are geometry, not matter. Softbodies addresses deformation; lsystems adds growth time.
capture_leaks.deterministic_randomness: Same seed = same tree. This is a gift (reproducible art) and a lie (real trees are not algorithmic). Stochastic L-systems soften this; true biological variance is never reached.
capture_leaks.scale_invariance_myth: Conceptually self-similar but not measurably so — the artifact has 3 levels, not a continuum. box_counting_dimension exposes the issue explicitly.

limit: Three levels of recursion, five main branches, four sub-branches each. The resulting geometry looks fractal; mathematically it’s just a finite tree. What this artifact captures: that recursion is a verb (call yourself), self-similarity is a consequence (child resembles parent), and bounded depth is the lie we tell to make infinity finite. What it cannot hold: true infinite fractals, physical growth, biological randomness, or fractal dimension as a measurable quantity. Each of those leaks has a home later.

grammar_alignment.note: recursive_tree teaches the meta-operation (call yourself with decremented depth) and subdivide-via-branching. The other three fractals operations are variations: delete (subtract at each level), iterate_complex (apply f to z), measure_dimension (count boxes across scales). This artifact is the genesis of all of them.

biome_alignment.note: Biome density 0.6 — life is visibly abundant. 'fractal' catalyst mode lets the player recurse on any form they pick up (a cube becomes a cube-of-cubes). 'grow_depth' verb dials depth up or down in real time. Trees in the biome now use real recursive generation; forest density has meaningful self-similarity.

stages.title: From local rule to self-reference
stages.thinking: CA_GameOfLife taught that simple local rules produce complex global behavior. Each cell looks only at its neighbors; emergent patterns come for free. Now a different move. Instead of many cells each following a local rule, ONE rule that calls ITSELF. No grid, no timestep. A function that produces form by asking: 'what would a smaller version of me produce?' Recursion is the mirror that turns a single rule into infinite structure.
stages.code:
# CA:
#   each cell: look at 8 neighbors, apply rule
#   complexity from many local decisions
#
# Recursion:
#   one function: generate_branch(length, depth)
#   which calls: generate_branch(length * 0.7, depth - 1)
#   which calls: generate_branch(length * 0.49, depth - 2)
#   ...
#   complexity from a function that remembers itself
#
# Two paths to emergence: distributed locality, vs self-reference.
# Both produce structures bigger than their rules.

stages.title: The trunk is the zeroth branch
stages.thinking: Start with the trunk: a single box mesh, rooted at origin, growing upward. This is the seed. In a tree of any depth, the trunk is the node that has no parent. Every other branch is a child. The code that draws the trunk is nearly identical to the code that draws any branch — which is why the next step can be recursive.

stages.title: The recursive call — the function becomes the tree
stages.thinking: generate_branches_from(origin, length, depth). For each sub-branch: compute its endpoint via rotated vector, create a box mesh between origin and endpoint, then call the same function from the endpoint with shorter length and decremented depth. The base case is depth == 0 (stop branching). Every tree is the trunk plus recursive calls from the top of the trunk. The function IS the tree.
stages.code:
func _generate_branches_from(origin: Vector3, length: float, depth: int) -> void:
	if depth <= 0:
		return  # base case: stop branching
	
	var branch_count = num_main_branches if depth == 3 else max_sub_branches
	
	for i in range(branch_count):
		# Each branch points in a random direction tilted from vertical
		var angle = randf() * TAU
		var tilt = randf_range(0.3, 0.9)  # radians from vertical
		var direction = Vector3(
			sin(tilt) * cos(angle),
			cos(tilt),
			sin(tilt) * sin(angle)
		)
		var end_point = origin + direction * length
		
		_make_branch_mesh(origin, end_point)
		
		# RECURSE: call self from the endpoint with shrunken params
		_generate_branches_from(end_point, length * 0.7, depth - 1)

stages.title: Deterministic chaos — seed makes reproducible trees
stages.thinking: The branches rotate at random angles — but if we call randf() repeatedly with no seed, every run produces a different tree. That’s fine for generative art, brutal for teaching. seed(42) at the start fixes the random sequence. Same seed, same tree, every time. Change the seed and you get a different tree from the exact same code. Seed 42 and seed 43 are two different forests that share a rule.
stages.code:
@export var random_seed := 42

func _ready() -> void:
	seed(random_seed)  # CRITICAL: must come before any randf()
	_build_trunk()
	_generate_branches_from(...)

# With the seed fixed, randf() is no longer random.
# It's a reproducible pseudo-random sequence.
# The tree becomes an expression of:
#   generate_branch(trunk_height * 0.7, depth=3) | seed=42
#
# Change seed to 7, to 1337, to int(Time.get_unix_time_from_system()):
# you get a gallery of trees from the same rule.

stages.title: Materials in three shades — trunk, branch, leaf
stages.thinking: Three StandardMaterial3D with emission: trunk_color (deep red), primary_color (brighter red for branches), secondary_color (red variation). Depth maps to material. The pedagogical effect: as your eye traces from trunk to canopy, color shifts subtly. The hierarchy is color-coded. Referenced from the Color sequence — we already know emission is glow, albedo is base, metallic is shine.
stages.code:
var primary_material: StandardMaterial3D
var secondary_material: StandardMaterial3D
var trunk_material: StandardMaterial3D

func _create_materials() -> void:
	trunk_material = StandardMaterial3D.new()
	trunk_material.albedo_color = trunk_color       # 0.8, 0.3, 0.3
	trunk_material.emission_enabled = true
	trunk_material.emission = trunk_color
	trunk_material.emission_energy_multiplier = emission_strength
	
	primary_material = StandardMaterial3D.new()
	primary_material.albedo_color = primary_color   # 0.95, 0.3, 0.3
	# ... emission, metallic, roughness same pattern

# Use material_depth_map:
func _material_for_depth(depth: int) -> StandardMaterial3D:
	match depth:
		3: return trunk_material
		2: return primary_material
		_: return secondary_material

stages.title: Rebuild on parameter change
stages.thinking: apply_grid_config or a slider modifies num_main_branches / max_sub_branches / random_seed. When that happens, clear all children and regenerate. The tree is not animated into existence; it is destroyed and reborn. This is the simplest correct pattern for deeply parameterized structures — rebuild is cheap at depth 3, and animation would require a separate system (deferred to L-systems sequence).

stages.title: Every subtree is a complete tree
stages.thinking: Here is the fractal property made explicit. Any branch in this tree, viewed in isolation, is itself a small tree: it has a root (where it attaches), a trunk (its own segment), and children (the sub-branches). The whole pattern repeats at every node. This is what self-similarity MEANS. Not 'looks the same' — literally IS the same thing, at a smaller scale. Zoom into any branch; you see a tree. Zoom further; you see a tree. Zoom enough (at infinite depth); you never find a 'last' tree.
stages.code:
# Consider the branch at depth 2:
#   it was created by _generate_branches_from(
#     origin = where its parent branch ended,
#     length = parent_length * 0.7,
#     depth = 2
#   )
#
# That call will create a mini-tree with depth-1 and depth-0 children.
#
# So the subtree rooted at any branch IS
# the same structure as the full tree — shrunk.
#
# SELF-SIMILARITY = the subtree is a complete tree.
# This is the definition of a fractal.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: The recursive tree knows what it is. Not a geometric sculpture — a rule that grows when asked. The critical parameter is num_main_branches (and by extension max_sub_branches) because branching factor is what makes the tree dense or sparse, lush or skeletal. The seed is the story. The depth is the lie. Each branch claims to be a tree and proves it by branching. What the artifact refuses: infinite depth, organic physics, biological variance, measurable fractal dimension. All of those are doors that open later.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: Procedural binary tree — a trunk forks into branches, each branch forks again, recursion depth 3. Box meshes with emission materials create a geometric canopy. Self-similar at every level.
# desire: To grow by halving — generate_branches calls itself with decremented depth, producing sub-branches from each endpoint. The tree is its own blueprint.
# critical_parameter: num_main_branches / max_sub_branches — control branching factor; random_seed — deterministic chaos, same seed same tree
# triggers: _ready → seed + material creation + full tree generation; rebuild_tree → clear all children, regenerate from parameters
# emerges: A geometric sculpture where every subtree is a complete tree — hierarchy from constraint, not command. Each node knows only its children yet the whole structure self-organizes.
# needs: VR branch manipulation [missing], growth animation [missing], parameter sliders [missing]
# relationships: Appears in DataStructures_Trees (binary recursion) and RecursiveEmergence_Tail_Recursion_Memoization (call stack visualization). The tree that teaches both data structure and recursion.
# truth: A tree is a list that learned to decide — left or right, less or greater. Hierarchy emerges not from authority but from the constraint of binary choice repeated.
